title: Theo and the Winter
premise: Folklorist Hazel Yarrow returns to the village of Wrenlow to record its winter songs, only to find that every household refuses to sing any verse twice — and that their childhood imaginary friend, Theo, is waiting on the porch, unchanged after twenty years. As the longest night approaches, Hazel discovers Theo is not imaginary but a thing the village once invited in through a lullaby, bound by a bargain renewed each generation with a song sung exactly twice. When Hazel's recordings accidentally complete the song, the bargain falls due, and they must survive until sunrise while uncovering which ancestor invited Theo in and why. In the end, Hazel chooses neither to renew nor destroy the bargain but to take Theo's memory into themselves, singing the song once more alone so it can finally be forgotten.
about_author: Ulyana Halloran grew up in a family of choir singers who believed certain hymns should never be repeated on the same day. She writes horror rooted in folk music, oral tradition, and the things families agree not to say out loud.

chapters.title: The Song You Don't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Hazel Yarrow arrives in Wrenlow with recording equipment and a grant proposal, interviewing elderly singers who each stop mid-verse, pale and refusing. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: unease dressed as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: What the Porch Remembers
chapters.summary: At the inherited family cottage, Hazel finds small footprints in frost leading to the door and a voice calling their childhood nickname. Theo stands waiting, unchanged since Hazel was nine. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: terror braided with longing.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Hazel catalogs rational causes — sleep paralysis, grief, carbon monoxide — while Theo sits patiently at the kitchen table describing Hazel's buried memories in perfect detail. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: the collapse of denial.

chapters.title: The Verse That Stops
chapters.summary: Hazel compares field recordings from other visits and finds every villager truncates the same winter carol at the same line. The missing verse is nowhere in any archive. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: scholarly dread becoming obsession.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous Won't Look Up
chapters.summary: The oldest singer, Mrs. Aldous, tells Hazel the carol is called the Inviting and warns them to leave before the solstice, then pretends deafness when pressed. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: first confirmation the village knows.

chapters.title: Theo's Favorite Game
chapters.summary: Theo proposes a game of hide-and-seek after dark; hiding, Hazel realizes the house itself seems to rearrange to help Theo seek. They escape to the churchyard at dawn. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: childhood comfort revealed as predation.

chapters.title: The Grange Book
chapters.summary: In the parish archive Hazel finds the Yarrow family grange book: an entry from 1898 recording 'the song sung twice, the door held open, the child given.' Their own great-grandmother's handwriting. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: inheritance curdling into guilt.

chapters.title: Everyone Was a Child Once
chapters.summary: Villagers admit, one by one, that each of them had an unchanged friend as children — always gone by age ten, always remembered as kind. POV: alternating villagers via Hazel's interviews. Emotional beat: collective complicity surfacing.

chapters.title: The Bargain's Terms
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldous explains: the Inviting brought warmth and good harvests; the price is one child's memory of their friend, paid when the song is sung twice. Hazel's recordings sang it twice. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: horror of accidental invitation.

chapters.title: Sunset Comes Early
chapters.summary: The solstice night begins unnaturally early; the sun stalls at the horizon and the village bars its doors. Theo knocks politely at Hazel's window. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: the long night opens.

chapters.title: Doors That Were Never Locked
chapters.summary: Hazel fortifies the cottage, but doors open for Theo because he was invited decades ago and invitations don't expire. He doesn't attack — he waits, and the waiting is worse. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: siege psychology.

chapters.title: The Tape Recorder Speaks
chapters.summary: Hazel plays back the night's recordings and hears a second voice beneath their own questions, answering in the missing verse. The machine has been translating Theo all along. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: evidence turning traitor.

chapters.title: What Theo Wants
chapters.summary: Theo confesses his purpose: not to harm Hazel but to be remembered, because being forgotten is the village's true cruelty — each generation erases him and calls it payment. POV: Hazel, listening. Emotional beat: sympathy as a trap.

chapters.title: The Missing Children
chapters.summary: Hazel cross-references parish records and finds nine children across two centuries who 'went to relatives' in winter and never appear again. All had the same friend. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: grief for the erased.

chapters.title: Midnight in the Churchyard
chapters.summary: Driven out by fire failing, Hazel crosses to the churchyard where the nine graves stand unmarked. Theo appears among them, naming each child lovingly. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: mourning weaponized.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous's Confession
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldous breaks her silence: her twin sister was taken in 1954, and she has sung the Inviting short ever since, starving Theo of renewal. Her defiance doomed the village schedule. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: anger at inherited sins.

chapters.title: The Choice Offered
chapters.summary: Theo offers Hazel the old terms inverted: remember him fully, take all nine children's memories too, and live — or forget everything, including their own childhood, and walk away whole. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: impossible arithmetic of self.

chapters.title: The Longest Hour
chapters.summary: Before dawn, time pools and thickens; Hazel relives the winter they were nine, seeing what actually happened when Theo left — the village singing him away mid-game. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: recovered memory as wound.

chapters.title: Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Hazel chooses a third path: they sing the Inviting themselves, both verses, twice through, claiming the bargain as the heir — binding Theo to them instead of the village. The house shakes; the frost recedes. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: climax of self-sacrifice and agency.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Dawn arrives ragged and real. Theo fades at the threshold, and Hazel, carrying every memory now, sings his name aloud so the village cannot pretend. Some weep; some slam windows. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: costly witness.

chapters.title: The Archive of Small Voices
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Hazel publishes nothing and destroys the tapes, instead building a private memorial book for the nine children, returned names and all. Belonging, they decide, means keeping what others buried. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: quiet reclamation.

chapters.title: Once More, for No One
chapters.summary: On the next winter solstice, Hazel returns to the cottage porch and sings the Inviting a single final time — a funeral, not an invitation — then lets the melody go. The footprints in the frost are simply footprints. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: release, memory kept without chains.
